DHS Equity Landscape
and Climate Report
From Hearts and Minds to Institutional and Structural Equity
Updated to include the One DHS self-directed equity resource platform strategy
Prepared by
Gary Banks
Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant
August 2026  |  Leadership companion report
Executive update: One DHS as equity infrastructure

Leadership finding. The One DHS prototype is a credible strategy for making trusted equity knowledge easier for DHS staff to find, understand, apply, and improve. Its promise is not simply that resources are placed on one website. Its value is that a governed platform can connect learning, tools, examples, reflection, practitioner expertise, and feedback at the moment staff need them.
Why this strengthens the climate strategy
It reduces friction created by scattered resources and inconsistent pathways to guidance.
It supports self-directed learning that staff can enter by task, role, question, or level of prior knowledge.
It converts practitioner expertise into durable organizational memory rather than leaving knowledge in isolated teams or individuals.
It gives equity tools a visible operational home while connecting users to human consultation when a resource alone is insufficient.
It creates a practical feedback loop in which staff questions, search behavior, and contribution patterns identify gaps in policy, guidance, training, and implementation.
Research validation

The approach is consistent with public-sector evidence and guidance. Digital.gov and the U.S. Web Design System emphasize user needs, accessibility, search, authoritative content, governance, measurement, and empowered content teams. CDC has implemented a self-guided, web-accessible Foundations of Health Equity training plan. OPM describes repositories, collaboration tools, and communities of practice as infrastructure for continuous learning, knowledge documentation, sharing, and innovation. GAO has repeatedly identified fragmentation, underused guidance, and the value of enterprise solutions, while also warning that a dashboard or platform must be evaluated through actual use, feedback, and mission value.
Conditions for responsible adoption
Governance: Name content owners, publication authority, review cadence, version history, and retirement rules.
Trust: Identify authoritative sources, dates, publication status, and the distinction between official guidance and community contribution.
Accessibility: Require keyboard and screen-reader testing, captions and transcripts, alternative text, readable structure, contrast, and document remediation.
Privacy and security: Collect no personally identifiable information for prototype use; establish approved upload types, moderation, records, retention, and security review.
Participation: Provide contribution and feedback pathways without implying that every submission is approved policy or guidance.
Measurement: Measure task success, time to trusted information, comprehension, confidence, application, accessibility, content freshness, and referrals for human support - not page views alone.
Recommended disposition

Continue as a governed, co-designed prototype. Use a bounded 90-day learning pilot before broader adoption. Expansion should remain conditional on demonstrated staff value, accessibility, content stewardship, privacy and security readiness, and a sustainable operating model.
Ninety-day learning pilot
Baseline: Confirm priority staff journeys, inventory current resources, and establish findability, confidence, and accessibility baselines.
Co-design: Test the experience with leaders, equity professionals, frontline staff, program staff, and people with different access needs.
Pilot: Release a governed collection for selected use cases, support it with office hours or consultation, and capture structured feedback.
Decide: Continue, revise, or stop based on evidence; define ownership, operating cost, and resource commitments before scale.
Pilot decision standard

Staff can find trusted resources faster, understand how to apply them, and identify when additional human support is needed. The platform also produces actionable evidence about missing, outdated, inaccessible, or difficult-to-apply resources.
Purpose, posture, and scope
Important framing

This observational report is not an attack on DHS leadership, its employees, or the equity work currently underway across the agency. It is a standard assessment and opportunity-forward document intended to complement the department's existing efforts. It is not written in opposition to, and is not proposed as a replacement for, DHS equity work. In the view of the Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant, that work is promising writ large. The purpose here is to help connect and strengthen it through a systemic and integrated framework - moving from Hearts and Minds equity, to institutional and structural analysis, to practical recommendations and reforms.

This report uses the term climate to describe the conditions in which equity work is understood, supported, implemented, experienced, and sustained. Climate includes the agency's stated commitments and the everyday signals that shape whether people believe those commitments are real: how decisions are made, whose knowledge counts, how burdens are distributed, what resources are available, how leaders respond to evidence, and whether communities and employees can see their influence in the system.

The report is designed for reflection, alignment, and action. It recognizes that DHS operates in a complex state-county-Tribal-provider environment and that some human services functions now sit across more than one state agency. It therefore focuses on the connections among policy, operations, data, workforce, procurement, accessibility, community partnership, and performance rather than assigning every outcome to a single office.

Scope and accuracy note. The report draws on the source material provided for this rewrite, including public information about DHS, the Department of Children, Youth, and Families, Minnesota's human services performance system, language and disability access requirements, procurement mechanisms, Medicaid equity work, MNbenefits, and the Olmstead planning process. Agency pages, statutory schedules, and program details should be rechecked before this report is used as a formal policy, legal, fiscal, legislative, or public accountability record.
Executive summary

DHS has meaningful equity foundations. Its strategic plan, Equity Policy, toolkit, performance-management work, language and disability access expectations, community partnerships, modernization efforts, and program-specific initiatives demonstrate that equity is already present in the department's formal direction and daily work. The central opportunity is not to start equity work over. It is to make the existing work more connected, visible, resourced, and consequential across the operating system.

The climate observed in the source material is best understood as a transition point. Hearts and Minds work - learning, intention, cultural awareness, reflection, and relationship-building - is necessary and promising. The next opportunity is to connect that work to the institutional structures that determine outcomes: policy and budget gates, technology design, eligibility and service workflows, data definitions, contracts, workforce systems, interagency agreements, and corrective-action routines.

A complementary equity operating system would allow DHS to answer five practical questions for any priority disparity: where is the burden or unequal outcome occurring; who has authority to change the condition; what resources and partners are required; how will progress be measured; and what will happen if the expected improvement does not occur?

The recommendations in this report are intentionally forward-looking. They call for an enterprise Equity Operations Council, an equity portfolio and stage gate, full client-journey mapping, reliable language and disability access, a cross-agency data and performance architecture, a DHS-DCYF operating compact, workforce and procurement reforms, paid lived-expertise partnership, a broader evidence standard, and durable rules, budgets, contracts, and routines.
How to read this report
Landscape: what the current equity climate appears to contain - strengths, signals, gaps, and opportunities.
Framework: how to connect Hearts and Minds equity to organizational practice, institutional design, and structural conditions.
Recommendations: practical reforms that complement DHS's current direction and can be prioritized by consequence and readiness.
Implementation: a staged 36-month pathway with decision gates, evidence requirements, and leadership questions.
References: source notes are consolidated at the end of the report; no inline citations are used in the body.
1. DHS equity landscape: the current climate

A useful equity landscape assessment begins with the organization as it operates, not with a generic description of diversity, equity, inclusion, accessibility, or anti-racism work. Minnesota DHS works through a network that includes state programs, counties, Tribal Nations, managed-care organizations, service delivery authorities, community providers, employees, and people who use human services. Equity climate is therefore produced across many locations and relationships.
1.1 Promising foundations

The source material reflects a substantial foundation on which to build. DHS has publicly articulated outcomes for people in Minnesota, for high-quality human services, and for employees who work in an inclusive environment. Its direction includes equitable and accessible service delivery, streamlined processes, partnership with Tribal Nations and counties, community voice, provider support, anti-racist and multicultural organizational development, psychological safety, wellbeing, and career pathways.

DHS also has an Equity Policy and Equity Analysis Toolkit that extend equity considerations beyond a single program. The policy context reaches into legislation, policy development, budgets, strategic planning, technology modernization, recruitment and retention, procurement, community engagement, and service delivery. The existence of these expectations is a strength because it positions equity as an agency responsibility rather than a discretionary add-on.

Other building blocks include MNbenefits, language and disability access requirements, human services performance measures, Medicaid equity work, disability and Olmstead planning, procurement opportunities for targeted vendors, and active child and family reforms. Collectively, these assets create a promising platform for a more integrated operating model.
1.2 The operating model is distributed by design

DHS cannot advance equity through one office or one training program alone. Many decisions that shape lived experience occur at program, county, Tribal, provider, technology, contract, or frontline levels. This distributed model makes local knowledge and partnership essential, but it also creates a risk: the department may have many good equity activities without one shared view of the outcomes, burdens, ownership, resources, and next decisions associated with them.

The opportunity is to establish a common minimum operating standard while preserving program-specific, Tribal, disability, cultural, linguistic, geographic, and community expertise. A common standard should clarify what must be analyzed, who decides, how affected people participate, what data is needed, how accessibility is assured, and how leadership will verify the result.
1.3 Current context that shapes the climate

Minnesota's human services performance-management experience suggests that a tool-centered approach is valuable for learning but may not be sufficient for sustained culture change or statewide scaling. The practical lesson is complementary: tools and training are important, and they are most effective when joined to coaching, change management, capacity, user groups, workflow ownership, and sustainability planning.

The movement of child and family functions into DCYF changes the accountability map without removing child welfare from the larger human services equity landscape. DHS remains connected through Medicaid, behavioral health, disability services, economic assistance, licensing, procurement, performance management, data infrastructure, and interagency coordination. Clarity about these relationships is a climate issue because organizational transitions can either strengthen shared accountability or create gaps that communities experience as fragmentation.

The Minnesota African American Family Preservation and Child Welfare Disproportionality Act creates a concrete opportunity to connect data disaggregation, family preservation, active efforts, case review, workforce practice, community oversight, and performance management. Its implementation should be approached as system change, with attention to service capacity and family experience as well as formal compliance.

2. Observations about the equity climate

The observations below are offered as constructive signals for discussion. They describe conditions that can occur even when employees and leaders are committed to equitable service and workplace outcomes. The distinction is important: an observation about system design is not a judgment about individual character or intent.
2.1 Intent and effect can diverge

A county eligibility worker may intend to treat people fairly while a process still produces unequal results if information is required in English, interpreter access is delayed, a narrow script limits judgment, or a missing document penalizes a delay outside the client's control. A social worker may value family preservation while the decision environment makes removal the easiest defensible option when services, housing, transportation, behavioral health, disability supports, or culturally responsive providers are unavailable. A hiring manager may value diversity while an unstructured interview rewards similarity and informal rapport.

The leadership question is therefore not only whether staff have good intentions. It is whether the system gives staff the tools, time, authority, information, support, and incentives to produce equitable results - and whether the department can detect and correct the moments when it does not.
2.2 Equity tools need a consequential home

An equity analysis or scan can be completed without changing the decision it examines. If review has no stage gate, no required response to identified harm, and no accountable owner, it can become documentation attached to a decision made elsewhere. The opportunity is to make every required analysis produce a disposition: approve, revise, pause, pilot, reject, or escalate.

A material unmitigated disparity should not be silently accepted. If leadership chooses to proceed, the decision should state why, what safeguards apply, who owns the risk, what data will be reviewed, and when the decision will be revisited.
2.3 Administrative modernization should be measured by total effort

MNbenefits is an important modernization that can simplify the first step for several economic-assistance programs. A more usable front door, however, does not automatically create an integrated service journey. Clients may still encounter different verification requirements, notices, account systems, contact channels, renewal processes, or appeals across programs and delivery partners.

The relevant equity measure is total effort from first contact to stable service: repeated requests, days waiting, abandoned applications, unresolved referrals, renewal interruptions, comprehension, and successful appeals. The opportunity is to treat MNbenefits as a platform for broader integration while maintaining human support through county, Tribal, phone, in-person, and community channels.
2.4 Rights must be experienced consistently

Language access and disability access are not only notice requirements. They are service conditions. A client must be able to understand what is being asked, communicate at the point of need, receive equally effective communication, use the relevant format or technology, and obtain assistance without carrying the burden of arranging it alone.

Because delivery is distributed across program areas, counties, Tribes, and providers, the same right can feel different from one channel to another. The opportunity is a department-wide minimum standard with a shared performance dataset, accessible materials, user testing, a remediation queue, and an escalation route for repeated failures.
2.5 Performance systems should make disparities actionable

A performance system governs what it defines, measures, reviews, and connects to improvement. If healthcare access, language access, disability access, client burden, culturally relevant quality, or intersectional outcomes are not measured, they remain outside the formal performance conversation. If a measure is suspended or retired while the underlying risk remains, an interim monitoring plan is needed.

The opportunity is to add an equity layer: disaggregated outcomes, disparity thresholds, qualitative evidence, client-burden measures, and corrective-action requirements. The absence of a measure should be treated as a measurement risk, not as evidence that no problem exists.
2.6 Community voice is strongest when it changes design

Listening sessions and advisory groups can build understanding, but participation becomes more credible when people can see how their knowledge changed a policy, budget, contract, service, or evaluation. The climate signal to watch is whether communities are asked to describe harm without receiving compensation, decision influence, accessible participation, or a response record.

The opportunity is to establish paid, accessible, longitudinal partnership. Community members, Tribal governments, disability leaders, culturally specific organizations, parents, youth, relatives, employees, and people who use services should be engaged at the level of influence required by the decision.
2.7 Training is necessary but not sufficient

Training can support understanding of laws, cultural context, accessibility obligations, data practices, trauma-informed principles, and structured decision tools. It cannot by itself remove a degree requirement, create a culturally specific provider, repair a data field, translate a notice, change a contract score, fund a navigator, or require a manager to correct a promotion gap. Training is most effective when it supports a changed operating environment rather than standing in for one.
3. From Hearts and Minds to institutional and structural equity
A complementary framework can be understood as four connected levels. Each level matters; none should be treated as a substitute for the others.
Level
What it asks
What makes it durable
Hearts and Minds
What do people understand, believe, notice, and practice in relationships?
Learning, reflection, cultural humility, trust-building, psychological safety, and leadership modeling.
Organizational practice
How do managers and teams make decisions and deliver services every day?
Clear workflows, structured decisions, coaching, accessible tools, workload capacity, feedback, and measurable expectations.
Institutional design
What do policies, budgets, contracts, technology, data, and governance make easier or harder?
Stage gates, resource commitments, data ownership, procurement standards, performance reviews, and corrective action.
Structural conditions
How do history, power, race, disability, culture, geography, income, language, and intersecting identities shape outcomes?
Disaggregated analysis, community power, cross-agency alignment, service capacity, and willingness to redesign the rules of the system.
Working principle

The strongest equity climate is one in which personal commitment and institutional design reinforce one another. Employees should not have to overcome a structurally inequitable process through individual goodwill, and leadership should not ask communities to trust an equity commitment that has no operating expression.

This four-level framework also clarifies the role of an Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant. The role is not to replace existing equity leadership, program expertise, Tribal sovereignty, disability expertise, community knowledge, or executive responsibility. It is to help connect those sources of knowledge to operational decisions, structural analysis, implementation, and measurable reform.
4. Complementary recommendations and reforms

The recommendations below are designed to strengthen and integrate work already underway. Each includes an objective, priority actions, evidence of progress, and primary ownership. They are intended to be sequenced according to consequence, readiness, capacity, and community guidance.
4.1 Establish an Equity Operations Council and executive stage gate
Objective. Create one governance mechanism that connects equity analysis to decisions, resources, risk management, and outcomes across DHS and relevant interagency partners.
Priority actions

Charter an Equity Operations Council chaired by an executive sponsor and including Equity and Inclusion, the Office of Indian Policy, Strategy and Performance, Employee Culture and Human Resources, Aging and Disability Services, Grants/Equity/Access/Research, procurement, IT, policy, legal, finance, program administrations, counties, Tribal Nations, labor, and community partners.

Maintain a single equity portfolio containing priority disparities, redesign pilots, policy reviews, procurement changes, workforce risks, data dependencies, community commitments, budgets, and corrective actions.

Establish an equity stage gate for policies, budgets, requests for proposals, major IT changes, service redesigns, and workforce initiatives. The gate should require a decision record, not only a completed scan.

Require each stage-gate record to identify affected populations, burden, benefits, alternatives, accessibility, language, Tribal and legal considerations, data needs, cost, owner, implementation date, and outcome measures.
Set an escalation rule: a material unmitigated disparity must be revised, piloted with safeguards, approved as an explicit exception by the responsible executive, or stopped.
Use quarterly reviews to examine whether approved actions occurred and whether the observed effect matches the expected effect.
Evidence of progress
A published charter, membership list, decision-rights matrix, and quarterly calendar.
A portfolio dashboard showing owner, status, risk, budget, milestone, and outcome for each priority action.
Sample policy, budget, IT, procurement, and workforce decisions with completed stage-gate records and documented disposition.
A corrective-action register showing unresolved disparities and the executive responsible for resolution.
Primary ownership. Commissioner's Office, in partnership with Equity and Inclusion and Strategy and Performance.
4.2 Turn MNbenefits into a full client-journey redesign
Objective. Reduce total administrative burden from first contact through verification, renewal, change reporting, appeal, and stable receipt of services.
Priority actions

Map the complete journey for a household applying for economic assistance, including transition from MNbenefits to county or Tribal processing, document submission, interviews, notices, case changes, renewal, and appeal.

Identify which adjacent programs are screened through the existing application and which remain outside the experience, including healthcare, MinnesotaCare, disability-related services, and other needs.
Define a cross-program referral standard: a clear explanation, warm handoff, contact, time expectation, and way to confirm that the handoff occurred.
Maintain human support through phone, in-person, county, Tribal, and community channels. Online convenience should not be treated as a replacement for accessible human assistance.
Fund Digital Navigators and community-based application support, especially in rural areas, Tribal communities, neighborhoods with limited broadband, and communities with limited English proficiency.
Rewrite notices and document requests so clients can identify what is needed, why it is needed, how to submit it, what happens next, and how to obtain language or disability assistance.
Measure total client effort, including contacts, repeated submissions, days waiting, abandoned applications, successful referrals, renewal churn, denials, appeals, and comprehension.
Evidence of progress
Current-state and future-state journey maps reviewed by clients, navigators, frontline workers, county and Tribal staff, accessibility experts, and program owners.
A list of programs inside and outside the MNbenefits experience with a documented referral or integration plan.
A client-effort dashboard disaggregated by language, race and ethnicity, disability, geography, age, and other relevant dimensions with privacy protections.
Verified reduction in repeated information requests, unresolved handoffs, abandoned applications, and renewal interruptions.
Primary ownership. Economic Assistance, Health Care, county and Tribal partners, IT, Strategy and Performance, and community navigation partners.
4.3 Operationalize language and disability access as service standards
Objective. Make free, timely, meaningful language assistance and equally effective communication reliable at every client contact, not only visible in notices or policy statements.
Priority actions

Adopt a DHS-wide minimum service standard: assistance is free, timely, available throughout operating hours, and never placed as a burden on the person with limited English proficiency or a disability.

Create a common performance dataset for interpreter requests, wait time, failed or delayed access, translated materials, language of service, client comprehension, accommodations, and complaint resolution.

Review county and provider language-access plans for operational readiness: who answers, who interprets, which languages are covered, how after-hours needs are handled, and how staff document service.
Standardize language-access and disability-access advisories in public materials while testing whether people understand the right and know how to request it.
Require document accessibility testing with screen readers, keyboard navigation, captioning, alternative formats, and disabled users before major publications or digital releases.
Create a centralized accessibility remediation queue with severity levels, owners, deadlines, and executive visibility. Program-area responsibility for cost should not mean program-area isolation.
Include access standards in contracts, requests for proposals, managed-care requirements, vendor monitoring, and provider technical assistance.
Evidence of progress
Interpreter and accommodation performance reported by program and county or Tribal delivery channel.
Priority forms, notices, web pages, videos, and training materials pass accessibility review with documented results.
Client testing shows that people can identify how to request assistance and understand information after assistance is provided.
Access failures have an owner, remediation date, and escalation path.
Primary ownership. Equity and Inclusion, civil rights, accessibility leadership, program administrations, county and Tribal agencies, IT, Communications, and procurement.
4.4 Build an equity data and performance architecture
Objective. Make disparities visible, interpretable, privacy-protected, and connected to management action across DHS, DCYF, counties, Tribes, and providers.
Priority actions

Create a cross-agency equity data dictionary covering race, ethnicity, culture, language, disability, gender, geography, income, age, and program-specific characteristics, with definitions, collection rules, missingness, and permitted uses.
Separate internal analytic capacity from public reporting. Use protected data for small-n and intersectional analysis while publishing safe aggregate trends and clear limitations.

Integrate equity measures into the Human Services Performance Management System, including client burden, language access, disability access, healthcare access, culturally relevant quality, and workforce outcomes.
Address gaps in healthcare access and effective-service measurement by developing measures with communities, counties, managed-care organizations, and people with lived experience.

For every measure, establish a baseline, threshold, improvement target, owner, reporting schedule, and corrective-action process. A suspended or retired measure should have interim monitoring if the underlying risk remains.
Use dashboards to identify disparities at decision points, not only final outcomes: screening, referral, approval, denial, wait, placement, service, renewal, and appeal.
Pair quantitative results with qualitative evidence, case review, community feedback, and frontline observation so data does not erase context.
Evidence of progress
An approved equity data dictionary and data-governance protocol.
A minimum set of equity measures added to each priority performance domain.
A dashboard with documented suppression rules, data-quality notes, and named owners.
Quarterly corrective-action reviews for measures that exceed disparity thresholds or show deterioration.
An annual review of which measures were used in budget, policy, procurement, workforce, or program decisions.
Primary ownership. Strategy and Performance, data governance, program analytics, Equity and Inclusion, DCYF where child and family data is involved, counties, Tribal Nations, and community partners.
4.5 Implement child-welfare equity reform through a DHS-DCYF operating compact
Objective. Ensure that the transfer of child and family programs strengthens rather than fragments accountability for disproportionality, family preservation, data, services, and community trust.
Priority actions

Create a written DHS-DCYF operating compact defining responsibilities for data sharing, Medicaid and behavioral-health linkages, disability services, benefits, procurement, workforce, performance management, community engagement, and public reporting.

Align measures with statutory categories such as representation, reporting, maltreatment, out-of-home placement, emergency removals, reunification, permanency, family connections, relative placement, disability, culture, income, and geography.

Treat active efforts and family preservation as operational requirements that require service capacity, culturally responsive safety planning, transportation, language access, housing support, behavioral health, disability supports, and relatives or kin who can participate.
Use structured decision-making and case review to identify where discretion, service availability, or court and agency practice leads to unnecessary removal or unequal treatment.

Make the African American Child Well-being Unit, Advisory Council, Tribal governments, community organizations, parents, youth, and relatives part of the implementation feedback loop with compensation and documented response.
Use the phase-in period to identify implementation barriers before statewide rollout rather than treating the phase-in as a compliance exercise.
Coordinate data definitions and reporting schedules so DHS, DCYF, counties, Tribes, and the public do not see conflicting versions of the same disparity.
Evidence of progress
A signed interagency compact and RACI matrix.
A joint dashboard or reporting package aligned with statutory categories and privacy rules.
Case-review findings linked to specific policy, training, service-capacity, or workflow changes.
Documented active-efforts and family-preservation implementation in phase-in counties.
A statewide readiness assessment before rollout.

Primary ownership. DHS and DCYF Commissioners' Offices, Child Safety and Permanency leadership, the Office of Indian Policy, counties, Tribal Nations, courts, providers, and community oversight bodies.
4.6 Redesign workforce entry, advancement, and retention
Objective. Make workforce equity measurable in recruitment, hiring, pay, promotion, acting appointments, performance feedback, accommodations, psychological safety, and retention.
Priority actions

Audit job classifications and minimum qualifications for unnecessary degrees, experience requirements, address or schedule assumptions, and barriers that exclude lived experience or community language and cultural knowledge.
Use trainee and paid-licensure pathways where jobs can be performed safely and effectively through training, supervised practice, and competency assessment.
Use structured interviews, common questions, scoring rubrics, diverse panels, and documented selection rationale. Monitor who advances at each stage.
Audit acting and interim appointments for transparency, rotation, access, and conversion to permanent positions.

Analyze time-in-class, pay, performance ratings, promotion, disciplinary action, developmental opportunity, and turnover by race, ethnicity, disability, gender, geography, and other relevant categories.
Create sponsorship for employees who are 'onlys' or 'firsts' in leadership roles, with executive actions rather than informal encouragement alone.
Treat Direct Support Professionals and Personal Care Assistants as a core equity and service-quality workforce. Track wages, benefits, vacancies, caseload, training, career progression, and turnover.
Require managers to have measurable DEIA goals that address outcomes or behavior, not merely attendance, and review those goals in performance management.
Evidence of progress
A workforce equity baseline and annual disparity report.
A structured-hiring protocol and acting-appointment audit.
Promotion, pay, and retention gaps with corrective-action owners.
Manager goals tied to measurable team conditions and service outcomes.
A burnout, workload, moral-injury, and secondary-traumatic-stress response plan.
Primary ownership. Employee Culture and Human Resources, Workforce Strategy and Planning, program leaders, labor partners, Equity and Inclusion, and Development and Learning.
4.7 Use procurement and grants to build community capacity
Objective. Make public spending a deliberate instrument for service equity, cultural fit, disability inclusion, geographic reach, and community wealth.
Priority actions
Use the state's targeted-group, economically disadvantaged, and veteran-owned vendor systems and Equity Select mechanisms as starting points for a DHS vendor-equity strategy.
Identify where solicitation size, insurance, cash flow, reporting, technical requirements, or prior-government experience exclude smaller and community-rooted organizations.

Revise RFP and grant rubrics to assign meaningful value to cultural and linguistic competence, lived experience, disability leadership, Tribal partnership, geographic access, family preservation, and measurable outcomes.

Provide pre-solicitation information sessions, proposal assistance, realistic payment terms, capacity-building grants, and technical assistance so community organizations can compete without imitating large institutions.
Require vendors to meet language, accessibility, data, complaint, and community-feedback standards, with resources to do so and consequences for repeated failure.
Analyze awards by vendor ownership, leadership, community served, geography, language, and contract value. Do not count diverse vendors without examining who receives meaningful and sustainable work.
Use contract renewals and performance reviews to determine whether providers actually reach the communities identified in the proposal.
Evidence of progress
A vendor-barrier assessment and revised solicitation templates.
Award and subcontracting data disaggregated by vendor type and community reach.
Payment-timeliness and capacity-building measures for smaller providers.
Contract monitoring that includes access, cultural fit, disability inclusion, and outcomes.
Primary ownership. Procurement, Grants, Equity and Inclusion, program administrations, the Office of Equity in Procurement, finance, legal, and community providers.
4.8 Institutionalize co-creation, trust repair, and lived expertise
Objective. Move communities from consultation recipients to paid partners who shape policy, program design, budgets, procurement, and evaluation.
Priority actions
Create a department-wide compensation policy for community expertise, including time, preparation, transportation, childcare, technology, interpretation, and accessibility costs.
Use a participation ladder that distinguishes informing, consulting, involving, collaborating, and empowering. Specify the level required for each decision.
Create longitudinal community partnerships rather than one-time listening sessions. Trust repair requires repeated, culturally specific engagement tied to policy and administrative activity.
Use community-defined measures of quality, trust, safety, dignity, and culturally relevant care alongside administrative outcomes.
Publish a response record that says what community members recommended, what changed, what did not change, and why.
Avoid extracting trauma. Do not ask employees or clients to disclose painful experiences as a substitute for paying experts, reviewing data, or redesigning the system.
Use compensated lived-experience participation in disability planning as a practical reference while adapting the approach to other communities and decision types.
Evidence of progress
A paid-lived-expertise policy and standard agreement.
A community-participation plan for every major equity redesign.
Documented changes to policy, budget, procurement, service, or evaluation resulting from participation.
Trust, comprehension, and perceived influence measures collected over time.
Primary ownership. Equity and Inclusion, the Office of Indian Policy, program administrations, community engagement, procurement, finance, and executive sponsors.
4.9 Expand the evidence standard without abandoning rigor
Objective. Recognize culturally adapted and community-defined practices as potentially valid evidence while maintaining safety, transparency, measurable outcomes, and ethical safeguards.
Priority actions
Distinguish between evidence that a model works in a population, evidence that a model is culturally acceptable and accessible, and evidence that a provider can deliver it safely.
Require cultural adaptation when a model was developed or tested in a population that differs materially from the people DHS is serving.

Accept practice-based evidence, community-defined outcomes, traditional healing, peer support, elders, doulas, and culturally specific organizations as evidence categories for review rather than dismissing them as unproven by definition.
Use community members and cultural experts to define meaningful outcomes while retaining independent review for safety, privacy, professional standards, and fiscal accountability.
Track whether conventional evidence requirements exclude providers that communities trust and whether funded models produce equitable results in practice.
Evidence of progress
A written evidence framework with definitions, review criteria, and examples.
Procurement and program documents that allow culturally specific and practice-based evidence.
Outcome monitoring that compares adapted and unadapted models where appropriate.
Community feedback on whether services are culturally relevant, safe, and effective.
Primary ownership. Program administrations, research and evaluation, procurement, legal, clinical and professional leadership, Equity and Inclusion, and community partners.
4.10 Make the work durable through rules, budgets, contracts, and routines
Objective. Prevent equity work from depending on a single leader, grant, training cycle, or political moment.
Priority actions

Identify which equity requirements belong in statute, administrative rule, policy, contract, grant agreement, budget instruction, performance plan, standard operating procedure, or technology requirement.
Use rulemaking and public notice when a durable, transparent requirement is appropriate; do not rely on an internal memo for a requirement that must survive leadership transition.
Assign recurring budget lines for accessibility, community compensation, data capacity, change management, evaluation, and frontline workload relief.
Embed equity outcomes in contracts, manager goals, program scorecards, procurement reviews, and annual planning.
Build succession and continuity plans for equity leadership, data ownership, community relationships, and high-risk pilots.
Publish annual status reports that distinguish completed activities, measured outcomes, disparities that remain, corrective actions, and decisions required from leadership.
Evidence of progress
A durability map showing the legal, budget, contract, policy, technology, and performance home for each intervention.
Recurring resource commitments rather than one-time project funds.
Continuity plans for key roles and partnerships.
Annual leadership reporting with unresolved disparities and explicit next actions.
Primary ownership. Commissioner's Office, policy, legal, finance, procurement, Human Resources, Strategy and Performance, and program leadership.
5. Thirty-six-month implementation blueprint

The blueprint is designed to support the department's current direction while reducing a common implementation risk: announcing a broad strategy, assigning it to a small office, offering training, and waiting for culture to change. Each phase has a distinct purpose, decision gate, and evidence requirement.
Timing
Purpose
Required work
Decision gate
0-90 days

Executive sponsor; Equity Operations Council charter; portfolio baseline; DHS-DCYF compact; data-access approvals; selected pilots; legal, privacy, accessibility, and Tribal review; community compensation protocol.
No pilot proceeds without a named owner, baseline, budget, affected-community plan, measure, and escalation path.
3-6 months
Map and design
Client journeys; high-discretion decision inventory; language and disability access assessment; workforce and vendor-barrier analysis; performance-measure design; community and frontline co-design.

Expand effective pilots; integrate stage gates into policy, budget, IT, procurement, hiring, and service delivery; implement child-welfare phase-in learning; build dashboards and corrective action.
Operating procedures, contracts, budgets, and performance systems reflect the new requirements.

5.1 Pilot selection criteria

Leadership should select pilots using criteria that prioritize consequence and learning value, not visibility. A strong pilot affects a high-consequence outcome, has an identifiable owner, can be measured within twelve months, involves people who experience the barrier, has a plausible intervention, and can be scaled if effective.

Evidence of disparate burden or outcome, with a feasible way to disaggregate or otherwise investigate it.
A defined decision point or workflow that can be changed.
A program owner with authority and capacity to implement.
Community, Tribal, frontline, disability, language, or labor partners who can shape the redesign.
A measurable baseline and a plan for privacy, accessibility, and unintended-effect review.
5.2 What should not be called progress by itself
Training completion without evidence of changed decisions, workflow, or outcomes.
A completed equity scan with no documented decision or corrective action.
A translated document when interpretation is unavailable at the point of need.
A dashboard that reports aggregate data and cannot identify or act on subgroup disparities.
A community meeting that produces no compensation, decision record, or change in design.
A diverse hiring slate without changes to selection, promotion, pay, retention, and psychological safety.
A diverse vendor count without meaningful awards, timely payment, community reach, or contract outcomes.
A new policy that says equity matters but does not assign a resource, owner, measure, or consequence.
6. Leadership scorecard

The scorecard should be reviewed quarterly by the executive sponsor and annually by the Commissioner or designated leadership body. It should show direction of change, distribution of outcomes across groups, and whether the department acted on what it learned.

7. Conclusion: a complementary path forward

DHS does not need to choose between the equity work already underway and the institutional reforms described here. The opportunity is to connect them. Strategic commitments, policy expectations, toolkits, performance systems, language and disability access, MNbenefits, Medicaid equity work, disability planning, procurement mechanisms, workforce efforts, community partnerships, and child and family reforms are important building blocks.

The climate question is whether those building blocks operate as a connected system. Can a person in Minnesota access, understand, influence, and benefit from human services without carrying a disproportionate administrative burden? Can employees enter, advance, contribute, and remain with fair opportunity and adequate support? Can public dollars build culturally responsive, accessible, and community-rooted capacity? Can leaders change course when data and communities show that a process is not working?

This report's proposed shift is from equity as an additional lens to equity as a design and performance requirement - while retaining the Hearts and Minds work that makes durable change possible. That shift does not diminish existing equity leadership. It gives existing commitments more structural support through executive authority, cross-agency coordination, data discipline, community partnership, accessible systems, procurement leverage, structured decisions, workforce investment, and durable rules and budgets.
Closing standard

The relevant test is not whether DHS has expressed care for equity. The relevant test is whether the department's operating conditions consistently turn that care into accessible services, fair opportunity, community influence, measurable improvement, and the willingness to redesign when outcomes show that more is needed.
